question: A patient in the active dying phase (last 24–48 hours) is no longer able to swallow oral medication. Their background morphine is 60 mg oral/day. What is the most appropriate next step regarding their opioid analgesia?

answers.text: Discontinue all opioids as the patient is now unconscious and cannot report pain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Discontinuing opioids risks undertreated pain and distress during dying. Unconscious patients may still exhibit signs of pain (grimacing, agitation). Opioids should be continued via an alternative route.

answers.text: Convert to subcutaneous morphine infusion using the oral:SC conversion ratio of 2:1 (i.e., 30 mg SC/24 hours)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The standard oral morphine to subcutaneous morphine conversion is 2:1 (oral dose halved). For 60 mg oral/day, the SC equivalent is 30 mg/24h via continuous subcutaneous infusion (CSCI/syringe driver), with SC breakthrough doses of 5 mg PRN.

answers.text: Convert to intravenous fentanyl using a 1:1 dose ratio with oral morphine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The fentanyl conversion is not 1:1 — fentanyl is approximately 100× more potent than morphine by weight. The subcutaneous route is preferred in palliative care; IV fentanyl requires specialist dose calculation.

answers.text: Prescribe rectal morphine suppositories at the same dose as the oral dose

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rectal morphine is an option but not standard first-line in palliative dying care. Bioavailability is variable, and the rectal route is often uncomfortable or unavailable. Subcutaneous infusion is the preferred route.

overallFeedback.feedback: When oral opioids are no longer feasible, convert to subcutaneous infusion using the 2:1 oral:SC morphine ratio. For 60 mg oral/day → 30 mg SC/24h via syringe driver, with 5 mg SC breakthrough doses PRN.
Correct. The oral:SC morphine conversion ratio is 2:1. A patient on 60 mg oral/day requires 30 mg SC/24h via CSCI — a standard palliative prescribing calculation (AS8.5).
